title: Modules: import and export
runtime: Modern evergreen browser or Node.js with ES modules. Run fragments in browser DevTools or a small .js file unless the example says otherwise.

objectives.text: Use modules to create explicit file boundaries.
Choose named or default exports deliberately.
Avoid hidden cycles and side effects.

sections.title: A module has its own scope
sections.body: An ES module is a file whose imports and exports state its dependencies and public values. Top-level declarations do not become global variables. In a browser, load an entry file with type="module"; in a build tool, the tool follows the same module graph.

sections.title: Exports form a public API
sections.body: Named exports keep the imported name connected to the exported name and allow several public values. A file can have one default export, imported under a chosen local name. Prefer a small, intentional public surface instead of exporting every helper.

sections.title: Imports are live bindings
sections.body: An import refers to the exporting module’s binding; it is not a copied variable that the importer can reassign. Browser relative paths need a correct relative URL and usually a file extension. Static imports are resolved before the module runs, while import() loads a module asynchronously.

sections.title: Think in a dependency graph
sections.body: Each import creates an edge between modules. Cycles can expose partly initialized values and make ownership unclear. Keep side effects in entry points, keep reusable modules focused, and move shared ideas into a lower-level module when two files depend on each other.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: Modules: import and export is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain modules: import and export to a junior developer.
interviewQuestions.answer: Use modules to create explicit file boundaries. Choose named or default exports deliberately. Import paths and bindings correctly. Avoid hidden cycles and side effects.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using modules: import and export behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can modules: import and export affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using modules: import and export produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
commonMistakes.cause: The underlying JavaScript behavior was not isolated first.
commonMistakes.fix: Reproduce the value or function behavior in a small JavaScript example, then reconnect it to the component.
